10.11 Endocrine System Impairment Evaluation Summary

Introduction

This chapter provides criteria for evaluating per-manent impairment of the endocrine system. The endocrine system is composed of the hypothalamic-pituitary complex; thyroid, parathyroid, and adrenals; islet cell tissue of the pancreas; and gonads. These ductless glands secrete hormones that regulate the activity of organs or tissues of the body. These hor-mones control growth, bone structure, sexual devel-opment and function, metabolism, and electrolyte balance. The various endocrine glands are usually interdependent, and a disorder of one gland may be reflected by dysfunction in one or more of the other endocrine glands, which, in turn, may affect other body systems. Consider multiple system effects when an endocrine permanent impairment is identified.

The following revisions have been made for the Sixth Edition: (1) the descriptions of endocrine gland function and of disease states have been updated, as well as the techniques for evaluation of these dis-eases; (2) the nomenclature of test procedures and of disease entities, such as diabetes mellitus, has been updated; and (3) a new method of impairment analy-sis has been provided along with multiple examples.

In brief, this new model accomplishes many of the goals set forth in Chapter 1. This model strives for internal consistency among the various endocrine disorders and reflects consensus statements derived from practicing internists and impairment evalu-ators. It also strives for a consistency of ratings between the various endocrinologic impairments and impairments in other organ systems.

Another change in this chapter is the inclusion of iatrogenic endocrinologic impairment. This change allows for the ability to rate the signs, symptoms, and physiological effects caused by medical treat-ment with hormonal agents. As an example, oral prednisone prescribed to control the signs and symp-toms of asthma can result in the individual develop-ing iatrogenic Cushing’s syndrome, which would then be rated as though the Cushing’s syndrome were a primary ratable disorder. If the prednisone were used to control 2 simultaneous disorders, such as occupational asthma and Crohn’s disease, appor-tionment issues will also be applicable (see Chapter 2). Sufficient details need to be supplied in the writ-ten report to support the inclusion of a rating for an iatrogenic endocrinologic disorder.

10.1 Principles of Assessment

Before using the information in this chapter, the Guides’ user should become familiar with Chapters 1 and 2 and the Glossary. Chapters 1 and 2 discuss the Guides’ purpose, applications, and methods of performing and reporting impairment evaluations. The Glossary provides definitions of common terms used by many specialties in impairment evaluations.

Dysfunction of an endocrine organ may be the result of an injury to the gland; of disease involving atro-phy, hypertrophy, hyperplasia, or neoplasia; or the result of a partial or total dysfunction of the gland by surgical removal, radiation, or medication. An endo-crine impairment develops from altered hormone levels by either oversecretion or undersecretion of the hormone or hormones by one or more endocrine glands and the effect of such hormonal aberrations on nonendocrine tissue. An endocrine impairment also develops from altered hormonal levels caused by exogenous administration. An impairment rating reflects the severity of the medical condition, the need for medication, the effects of the discontinu-ation of these medications, and the effects of the impairment on the individual’s ability to perform Activities of Daily Living (ADLs). As stated in Chapter 1, even with appropriate medication, some individuals will never regain their previous health

status irrespective of the efficiency of the hormone replacement or suppression.

When an endocrine disorder results in decreased secretion of a hormone, it is usually possible to replace the hormone by either the oral or the paren-teral route, resulting in virtual normalization of body physiology. In cases where the replacement hormone does not completely mimic the normal hormonal state, the individual may be given an impairment rating to reflect the signs, symptoms, or the changes that occur in his or her normal daily activities cre-ated by the residual hormonal insufficiency.

Disorders resulting in an increased secretion of a hormone are often amenable to effective treatment. In some cases, the treatment may leave the indi-vidual with a reduced ability to secrete the hormone, requiring replacement hormone. This situation is then similar to that of the patient who presents with a hormonal deficiency. In other cases, the condi-tion can only be treated incompletely or not at all. Impairment then is assessed based on the physiologic consequences of the hormone excess, its effects on other organ systems, and the disturbances in the person’s ADLs created by the signs and symptoms of the hormone excess.

Endocrine deficiencies may cause or be associ-ated with impairments of other organ systems. Impairment ratings in other body systems are evalu-ated separately and then combined with the impair-ment rating from this chapter, using the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix to determine the esti-mated whole person impairment (WPI).

10.1a Methodology for Determining the Grade in an Impairment Class

This chapter employs impairment grids to use in determining the appropriate impairment class (class) and severity grade (grade) within a class for the condition or conditions being rated at Maximum Medical Improvement (MMI). As was stated in chap-ter 1, the decision regarding which factor is the pri-mary determinant of impairment (key factor) will be clearly stated in each organ system impairment grid. For this chapter on the endocrine system, history will usually serve as the key factor. The examiner will use this key factor to determine the appropriate class with the middle grade (integer) in that class as the initial (default) rating (see Table 10-1). The exam-iner will then use non-key factors to assign grades for factors other than that considered “key,” with it being impossible to move upward or downward between classes based on these non-key factors. The number of potential grades for each impairment class varies based on the number of relevant factors.

When there are 2 non-key factors, there are generally 5 impairment grades per class; the presence of only one relevant factor other than the key factor reduces the number of possible grades to 3 per class.

If the examiner determines that the other factors affecting the rating are in the same class that had been used for the key factor rating, the final rating will generally stay in the middle of that class. On the other hand, if the classes chosen are higher or lower than that used for the baseline impairment rating, the level will be moved to the right or to the left (to a higher or lower value) to reflect the numerical discrepancy. For example, if the key factor places the initial rating in class 3, grade C and there are 2 non-key factors (lead-ing to a total of 5 possible grades) that are in class 1 and class 4, respectively, the first factor would move the grade down 2 levels to grade A and the second would move it back up 1 level to grade B. However, if both non-key factors were class 1, the rating could not go any lower than class 3, grade A, the lowest value for the class. An exception to this rule may occur when the key factor is in the highest impairment class for the disorder, as non-key factors falling in the same class can be used to adjust the impairment rat-ing upward to the highest grade within the class rather than keep it at the middle level. Specific tables will indicate if a rating schema other than this is used.

Unless otherwise specified, the history will be the “key factor” used in all the tables in this chapter. In most circumstances, it is the only factor. The physi-cal examination is generally of little value when the systemic impact of endocrinologic conditions has been mitigated by appropriate medical treatment. Likewise, objective tests are useful in endocrinologic disorders but are of limited value when used to define the degree of severity of a particular condition. Their primary utility is to help diagnose the disorder and to ascertain the completeness of treatment goals (rather

than predict response to treatment). For example, in those individuals with hypothyroidism, infinite levels of hormone deficiency may exist ranging from com-plete (as in the person with the total thyroidectomy) to extremely mild, depending on the amount and degree of pathology in the diseased gland. Yet all are amena-ble, in most circumstances, to complete treatment with a simple medication that will remove all the signs and symptoms of the disorder, returning the person to a completely functional state.

The same rules provided in the tables in this chapter apply when rating a pharmacologic hormonal excess due to the administration of a hormonal agent. The report must document: (1) the treated impairing dis-order, (2) the need for this form of treatment, (3) the (relative) permanency of this form of treatment, (4) the relationship between this form of treatment and the attainment of MMI, and (5) other issues as clari-fied in each of the subsections of this chapter. The only issue that will not apply to the rating of cases of hormonal excess caused by exogenous adminis-tration is the need to establish the “presence of” an anatomic or physiological causation.

10.1b Interpretation of Symptoms and Signs

The endocrine system has a wide array of glands, each with specific functions. These signs and symptoms are discussed in the section pertaining to each gland.

10.1c Description of Clinical Studies

Clinical studies for the endocrine system generally assess hyperfunction (increased) or hypofunction (decreased) of a specific gland, and are discussed in detail in each section. Additionally, imaging studies can be used to detect anatomic glandular abnormali-ties such as hypertrophy (hyperplasia), nodules, and tumors, both benign and malignant.

10.1d Specific Methodology for Impairment Rating in Endocrine Disorders

For the reasons discussed earlier, the historical por-tion of the impairment tables will be the “key fac-tor” used to determine the impairment rating. The tables contain, in addition to the history, impairment classes that are based on the “Burden of Treatment Compliance” (BOTC), which include the therapeutic procedures necessitated by the endocrine disorder. In the endocrine chapter, the BOTC is generally used as the primary discriminator of the level of impairment within the class to which the patient was assigned based on his or her clinical history.

At times, the more severe an endocrine disorder or the longer that it is present, the greater are the chances that the disorder will affect other organ systems. For example, the person with long-standing diabetes will have a greater risk of atherosclerotic consequences. These secondary consequences should be rated using the chapter that corresponds to the appropriate organ system.

The field of endocrinology encompasses multiglan-dular disorders. For consistency in this edition of the Guides, all endocrinologic impairment is combined when addressing the effects of the various glands and/or hormones. For example, say a person has a multihormonal deficiency caused by a pituitary problem, the clinical evaluation is completed, and the person has attained MMI. In this case, each hor-monal deficiency is rated separately using the rules found in this chapter for each of the components of the endocrine system, and then these values are combined.

The primary function of endocrine glands is to modulate the function of other organ systems. Thus, any impairment created by a hormonal perturba-tion is usually reflected in the impairment of the target organ system that the hormone modulates. As a result, the impairment ratings in the endocrine system are generally lower than the ratings found in other organ systems.

When the individual has attained MMI and has residual symptoms or physical findings, impair-ment could be assessed by another organ system or systems, by the endocrinologic condition, or by both methods. For example, a woman is slightly hyperthyroid when at MMI. She has a mild resting tremor, tachycardia, and anxiety. If the Central and Peripheral Nervous System, Cardiovascular, and Mental and Behavioral Disorders chapters (Chapters 13, 4, and 14, respectively) completely rate each of these residual problems, then she should not be

considered as having an endocrinologic residual (as used in the tables found in this chapter) and her endocrine impairment rating will primarily reflect her BOTC. If, on the other hand, residual problems are not encompassed by other chapters, the patient should be rated as though meeting the definition of having endocrinologic “residuals.” If these problems are attributed to and rated by this chapter, the ratio-nale needs to be adequately explained in the report.

10.1e Impairment Based on Burden of Treatment Compliance

As introduced in Chapter 1, impairment based on the BOTC model is a reflection of the impact on ADLs. Given the degree to which medical and dietary regimens (which are at times demanding) can fully compensate for even a complete loss of intrinsic endocrine function (and prevent most, if not all, systemic sequelae), it would appear reasonable to recognize and provide an impairment rating for the “burden” of patient compliance with these regimens. This is especially true given that optimal control of diseases such as diabetes often requires patients to adhere to a strict regimen of injections, medications, and blood testing, all of which may require adjust-ment based on the degree to which diet and activity levels remain constant. This chapter consequently goes into far more detail regarding the BOTC than was seen in other chapters.

1. Medications: BOTC points are assessed reflect-ing the frequency of use and the route of administration.

2. Dietary modifications: BOTC points are assessed when dietary control is needed to control or mod-ify an endocrinologic disorder.

3. Procedure-based impairment (PBI): BOTC points are assessed reflecting the consequences of bodily invasion for maintaining control over the endocri-nologic disorder.

4. Surgical intervention: Surgical intervention that is necessary to treat and/or control an endocri-nologic condition is considered as a treatment in this chapter. Although not necessarily accruing BOTC points for use in the tables found in this chapter, surgical interventions allow for inclu-sion into appropriate sections of the tables found in this chapter described as “needing treatment.” Thus, an individual who required surgical treat-ment for an endocrinologic disorder will always be considered as “having received required treat-ment”; placing that individual into class 0 would be inappropriate.

10.1f Rules for use of Burden of Treatment Compliance in this Chapter

Medication Use

Perform the following analysis to determine the BOTC score due to medication use:

1. Determine the route of administration for medica-tions and select the appropriate table. Use Table 10-2a for all medications given by the enteral, intranasal, and topical routes. Use Table 10-2b for all medications given by the parenteral routes. If there is more than 1 medication for either route of administration, use the medication with the great-est dosing frequency.

2. Determine the points for each medication based on the dosing frequency.

3. Add the points from Tables 10-2a and 10-2b to get a total score for medications.

Use Tables 10-2a and 10-2b for determining points for frequency and route of medications.

Dietary Modiﬁ cation

Some endocrinologic conditions require dietary modifications. The degree to which the dietary modifications are necessary varies from patient to patient, as does the degree to which patients comply with these modifications. The BOTC points are assessed for dietary modification when the patient is compliant with these modifications. They are based on the premise that complying with dietary restrictions restricts ADLs in ways other than those measured by the history and med-ication use alone. (See Table 10-3).

Procedure-Based Impairment (PBI)

Points in this section are awarded for procedures based on the interferences in an individual’s ADLs created by the need for monitoring of the endocri-nologic condition. Currently, this method of impair-ment assessment is defined only for blood glucose monitoring for the diabetic individual but can be used as a model if other types of monitoring for a different endocrinologic condition exists. 10.1g Rules for the Determination of Endocrinologic Whole Person Impairment

1. Choose the appropriate class of impairment based on the gland involved and clinical history (key factor). Begin with the middle level of impairment for the class.

2. Calculate the points and respective class for BOTC and use the class in which the BOTC points fall to modify the WPI upward or down-ward within the initial impairment class.

3. Use any other key factor that may be present to further modify the impairment rating (grade).

4. Combine with any other endocrinologic impairment.

10.2 Hypothalamic-Pituitary Axis

The hypothalamus and the pituitary are regarded as a unit because of their interdependent function. The hypothalamus produces chemical factors that either inhibit or enhance production of anterior pituitary hormones. The hypothalamus also produces antidi-uretic hormone (ADH) and oxytocin, which travel

through neural axons and are stored in the posterior pituitary. The anterior lobe of the pituitary gland, with modulation by the hypothalamus, produces tro-phic hormones that control the activity of the thyroid gland (thyrotropin [TSH]), the adrenal gland (corti-cotrophin [ACTH]), and the gonads (luteinizing hor-mone [LH] and follicle-stimulating hormone [FSH]). The chemicals produced by the hypothalamic-pitu-itary axis (HPA) are thus divided into “full” or final hormones (with full expression of effect), prohor-mones (that are precursors of the final hormone), or trophic hormones (that produce their final effect by inducing the secretion of the final hormone, that can express the “full” effect of the hormone, from a dif-ferent gland).

Hypothalamic substances also modulate the produc-tion of growth hormone (GH) and prolactin in the anterior lobe of the pituitary gland. These 2 hor-mones, however, exert their effects directly on the tissues of the body rather than through stimulation of other hormones. Growth hormone is responsible for growth of the skeleton before epiphyseal closure and, in the adult, maintains normal fat, muscle, glucose, and skeletal metabolism, as well as a sense of well-being. For women, prolactin is necessary for lacta-tion following delivery and for milk production in the suckling process.

The posterior lobe of the pituitary is an extension of hypothalamic neurons. It is the location where ADH (vasopressin) and oxytocin are converted from their prohormone state and released into the blood. Antidiuretic hormone regulates the fluid balance of the body through its ability to influence the excre-tion of water. The actions of oxytocin may have a role in the process of labor and lactation. Permanent impairments due to altered function of the thyroid gland, adrenal glands, gonads, and GH are discussed in subsequent sections of this chapter.

10.2a Interpretation of Symptoms and Signs

The HPA may be associated with visual field abnor-malities, which are considered in Chapter 12, The Visual System. Problems with the HPA may also present with temporal lobe seizures, frontal lobe abnormalities, obstructive hydrocephalus, and non-endocrine hypothalamic dysfunction, which are con-sidered in Chapter 13, The Central and Peripheral Nervous System.

Hypersecretion by the anterior lobe hormones is caused by microadenomas or macroadenomas. Prolactin excess results in hypogonadism. In women, this may lead to amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea, infertility, varying degrees of estrogen deficiency

with its detrimental effect on the vascular and skel-etal systems, decreased libido, and galactorrhea. In men, it may result in decreased libido, impotence, or infertility. Impairment from prolactin excess is equivalent to gonadotropic deficiency of the appro-priate end-organ, that is, secondary ovarian failure in women and testicular failure in men. Gonadal failure is discussed further in Section 10.8 of this chapter.

Gigantism results when GH hypersecretion occurs before epiphyseal closure; when GH hypersecre-tion occurs in the adult, acromegaly results. The manifestations of acromegaly include enlargement of the hands and feet, coarseness of facial features, prognathism, fatigue, and increased perspiration. Acromegaly of long duration may lead to degenera-tive arthritis, peripheral neuropathy, insulin resis-tance and glucose intolerance, and shortened life expectancy resulting from cardiovascular disease. Survival in the acromegalic patient is reduced, on the average, by 10 years due the cardiovascular con-sequences. Controversy exists regarding an excess of colonic neoplasia.

Hyposecretion of a single or of multiple anterior lobe hormones is known as hypopituitarism, and the deficiencies may be either partial or complete. In the adult years, pituitary tumors, infarction (espe-cially postpartum infarction), infiltrative disease, granulomatous disease, head trauma, and surgical or radiotherapeutic interventions are the most common causes.

In adults, hypopituitarism most often results in hypo-gonadism and a deficiency of GH production. The most common symptoms of hypogonadism in men are impotence, weakness, decreased motivation, and depression. The most common presenting symptom of hypogonadism in women is amenorrhea. Growth hormone deficiency is accompanied most often by muscle weakness and reduced exercise capacity, fat accumulation (especially intraabdominal), decreased bone density, lack of motivation, a poor sense of well-being, and social isolation. Postpartum pituitary infarction also results in an inability to lactate due to low levels of prolactin. Hypopituitarism in a person with diabetes mellitus results in decreasing insulin requirements with an increased incidence of hypo-glycemic episodes. Effects of dysfunction of TSH and ACTH secretion will be discussed in Sections 10.3 and 10.5, respectively.

Hyperfunction of the posterior lobe, which causes an excess of vasopressin or the syndrome of inap-propriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), may result from a variety of central nervous system disorders; however, SIADH is rarely permanent.

Inability of the kidneys to secrete a water load leads to hyponatremia if water intake is not restricted. Fatigue and lethargy, progressing to confusion, coma, and seizures, may result based on the degree of hyponatremia.

Hypofunction of the posterior lobe results in ADH deficiency and diabetes insipidus. Hypofunction usu-ally stems from diseases involving the hypothalamus or pituitary stalk and, less commonly, from diseases of the pituitary gland itself. The hypofunction may be hereditary, or it may be related to trauma, surgery, metastatic tumors, craniopharyngioma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, and sarcoidosis. If the thirst response is normal, diabetes insipidus is mostly an inconvenience because of polyuria, polydipsia, and nocturia. Severe dehydration and hypernatremia may result if the inability to ingest an adequate amount of fluid ensues or if thirst is impaired because of concomitant hypothalamic disease. This can lead to central nervous system changes, for example, mental depression or coma.

10.2b Description of Clinical Studies

Structural abnormalities are evaluated by roentgeno-grams of the sella turcica, computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), espe-cially with gadolinium. Angiography occasionally is required. Evaluation of visual fields may be needed; vision impairments are discussed in Chapter 12, The Visual System.

Hormonal function must be assessed, and this is often done by stimulation or suppression testing. Growth hormone deficiency is assessed by measur-ing GH in the blood after stimulation testing with GHRH (growth hormone–releasing hormone). Corticotropin deficiency is assessed by measuring serum corticotropin and cortisol levels and by stimu-lation testing with insulin or corticotropin-releasing hormone. The diagnosis of secondary hypothyroid-ism (pituitary and hypothalamic hypothyroidism) is made by demonstrating low concentrations of thyroid hormones without elevation of the thyrotro-pin level. Secondary gonadal insufficiency, that is, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, requires the dem-onstration of end-organ failure, with low testosterone levels in men and low estrogen levels in women, as well as low or normal levels of the gonadotropins LH and FSH. Insufficiency of ADH requires the documentation of urine hyposmolality in the face of a stimulus to concentrate urine, usually water restric-tion. Prolactin deficiency is diagnosed by low basal levels of prolactin and its failure to increase after an injection of stimulating agents.

Growth hormone excess is documented by elevated insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1), also called somatomedin-C, and by the failure to suppress GH concentration after a glucose load. Prolactin excess is documented by measurement of elevated basal levels of prolactin. Inappropriate secretion of ADH is documented by hyponatremia with inappropriately elevated urinary osmolality and sodium levels, in the presence of normal cardiac, renal, adrenal, and thy-roid function.

10.2c Criteria for Rating Permanent Impairment due to HPA Disorders

The assessment of permanent impairment of the whole person from disorders of the HPA requires evaluation of (l) primary abnormalities related to GH, prolactin, or ADH; (2) secondary abnormalities in other endocrine glands, such as the thyroid, adre-nal, and gonads; and (3) structural and functional disorders of the central nervous system caused by anatomic abnormalities of the pituitary. The exam-iner must evaluate each hormonal disorder sepa-rately, using the guidelines in this chapter for each of the hormonal abnormalities that exist because of an HPA disorder. These values are then combined to produce the final endocrinologic impairment rat-ing for the HPA disorder. Following this step, the impairment of other abnormalities in close anatomic approximation to the hypothalamus and pituitary gland are evaluated and rated such as those causing impairment in the visual system (Chapter 12), central and peripheral nervous system (Chapter 13), or those

causing mental and behavioral disorders (Chapter 14). The estimated impairments of the various organ systems then should be combined by means of the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix.

Table 10-5 is to be used in those cases of a hormonal disorder due to an HPA disorder. It is to be used for those hormones or prohormones that are produced by the HPA. It is not to be used for abnormalities of the trophic hormones (TSH, ACTH) produced by the HPA. For the impairment assessment of those abnormalities, other sections of this chapter should be used. For example, if a person has an abnormality of the GH (“full” or final hormone) or ADH precur-sor (prohormone), Table 10-5 is to be used to assess the impairment. However, if a person has an abnor-mal secretion of their ACTH because of an HPA disorder, the endocrinologic impairment is assessed using the adrenal cortex section of this chapter (Section 10.5). In those cases in which a trophic hormone is rated by another section of this chapter, the portions of the appropriate table requiring “the presence of — disorder” is waived based on the “presence of a disorder” of the HPA. Thus, if a per-son has central hypothyroidism (caused by a lack of thyroid- releasing hormone), the individual is rated by the thyroid section of this chapter (Section 10.3) as if his or her primary disorder were based on a disorder of the thyroid gland.

EXAMPLE 10-1: TRAUMATIC DIABETES INSIPIDUS

Subject: 19-year-old man.

History: Head trauma from a motor vehicle crash 15 months earlier. Fluid intake and output ranged from 4 to 7 L/d.

Current Symptoms: Severe thirst; increased fre-quency of urination. Nocturia occurred 3 to 6 times, and thirst during the night is marked. General health excellent except for fatigue related to interrupted sleep. Symptoms controlled by treatment but recur if a dose of desmopressin is missed. No symptoms of other endocrine disease found; able to carry out ordi-nary daily activities.

Physical Exam: Normal.

Clinical Studies: On initial assessment, serum osmo-lality: 292 mmol/kg H2O (292 mOsm/kg H2O); serum sodium concentration: 142 mmol/L (142 mEq/L); urine osmolality: 120 mmol/kg H2O (120 mOsm/kg H2O); specific gravity: 1.003. No glycosuria. Attempt at water deprivation led to severe thirst with a serum osmolality of 302 mmol/kg H2O (302 mOsm/kg H2O) and urine osmolality of 150 mmol/kg H2O (150 mOsm/kg H2O). After an initial ADH injec-tion, urine osmolality rose to 450 mmol/kg H2O (450 mOsm/kg H2O) and urine volume diminished. Placed on a regimen of desmopressin, 0.1 mL (10 μg) twice daily by nasal spray; on this regimen, feels well and urine output is well controlled.

Diagnosis: Traumatic diabetes insipidus controlled by treatment.

Treatment: Desmopressin, 0.1 mL (10 μg) twice daily by nasal spray; no water restriction.

BOTC: Two BOTC points are given for the use of intranasal medication twice a day with no dietary modification or PBI points.

10.3 Thyroid

10.3a Interpretation of Symptoms and Signs

The thyroid gland hormonally influences the meta-bolic rate of many organ systems. Hypersecretion (ie, hyperthyroidism) is manifested by nervous-ness, weight loss, heat intolerance, goiter, tachycar-dia, palpitation, atrial fibrillation, frequent bowel movements, tremor, and/or muscle weakness.

Hyposecretion (ie, hypothyroidism) is manifested by lethargy, mental process slowing, weakness, cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, and/or myx-edema. Late hypothyroid complications include myo-cardial insufficiency, effusions into body cavities, and coma.

10.3b Description of Clinical Studies

Clinical studies include but are not limited to a determination of: (1) circulating thyroid hormone levels, including total thyroxine, free thyroxine, triiodothyronine, and free triiodothyronine; (2) cir-culating pituitary thyrotropin level; (3) radioiodine uptake of the thyroid gland; and (4) thyroid antibod-ies. The nature of thyroid nodules is often best evalu-ated by needle aspiration followed by surgery in appropriate cases.

10.3c Criteria for Rating Permanent Impairment due to Thyroid Disease

In practically all individuals with hyperthyroid-ism, the condition can be corrected by treatment and there is no loss in the ability to perform ADLs. However, the ophthalmopathy seen in some patients with hyperthyroidism caused by Graves’ disease may persist after treatment of the thyrotoxic state and result in permanent cosmetic disfigurement and/or visual impairment. In severe cases, loss of vision may result. These conditions should be evaluated as described in the chapter on the visual system (Chapter 12). Atrial fibrillation that persists following adequate treatment of hyperthyroidism should be evaluated as described in the chapter on the cardiovascular system (Chapter 4). In most instances, hypothyroidism can be controlled satisfac-torily by the administration of thyroid medication. Occasionally, because of associated disease in other organ systems, full hormone replacement may not be possible. In those circumstances, the endocrine impairment will reflect the incomplete nature of the treatment. History is the key factor. See Table 10-6.

10.4 Parathyroids

The secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH) from the 4 parathyroid glands regulates the levels of serum calcium and phosphorus that are essential to the proper functioning of the skeletal, digestive, renal, and nervous systems. The major abnormalities of these glands include hyperfunction, hypofunction, and carcinoma.

10.4a Interpretation of Symptoms and Signs

Hypersecretion of PTH, or hyperparathyroidism, may be due to the hyperfunctioning of 1 gland, as with an adenoma, or of all 4 glands, as with hyper-plasia, or may result from a parathyroid carcinoma. Manifestations of this condition include lethargy, constipation, nausea, vomiting, polyuria, and, in extreme cases, bone pain, renal calculi, renal failure, and coma. Hyposecretion of PTH, or hypopara-thyroidism, may be congenital in origin or due to inadvertent removal of the parathyroid glands dur-ing thyroidectomy, surgical excision for the treat-ment of hyperparathyroidism, or unknown causes. Manifestations include chronic fatigue, paresthesia, tetany, and seizures. Additionally, in cases of chronic hypocalcemia, there may be cataracts, eczema-tous dermatitis, alopecia, and abnormal dentition. Hypoparathyroidism may also coexist with hypo-function of other endocrine organs caused by poly-glandular autoimmune deficiency that might present with hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus, adrenal insufficiency, hypogonadism, and pernicious anemia.

10.4b Description of Clinical Studies

Techniques for evaluating parathyroid gland function include determinations of serum calcium (including ionized calcium), phosphorus, albumin, creatinine, magnesium, PTH levels, 1,25(OH)2 vitamin D, calcium concentration in urine, and urinary calcium to creatinine 24-hour clearance ratios. Intravenous pyelography, skeletal roentgenography, renal

ultrasound, and bone density studies may be use-ful. Sestamibi scanning with or without iodine 123 (I123) subtraction as well as ultrasonography, MRI, and CT are all useful tools in localizing parathyroid adenomas.

10.4c Criteria for Rating Permanent Impairment due to Parathyroid Disease

In most cases of hyperparathyroidism, surgi-cal treatment results in correction of the primary abnormality, although secondary symptoms and signs may persist, such as fracture, renal calculi, or renal failure. The latter signs should be evaluated according to criteria in the chapters dealing with the musculoskeletal system (Chapters 15 through 17) or the urinary and reproductive systems (Chapter 7). If surgery fails, or if the individual cannot undergo sur-gery, long-term therapy may be required. The signs and symptoms of hypoparathyroidism are generally correctable with calcium and vitamin D supplemen-tation. For those individuals who have persistent and refractory hypocalcemia, there may be multiple organ system manifestations, as discussed earlier. The individual should be rated by those organ sys-tems, as opposed to a primary rating in this section unless there are signs and symptoms that are not rated by other chapters, such as the person who pres-ents with residual paresthesia or fatigue.

Note: The “residual signs” of a parathyroid disor-der, as used in other sections of this chapter, refers to symptoms that are not rated by a different organ

system. The physical examination findings that are included in Table 10-7 refer to those abnormalities that can be explained by uncorrected abnormalities in the serum calcium. If another chapter rates all the residual signs and symptoms, the examiner uses a lower parathyroid class. Rarely will an adenoma give rise to local symptoms due to a mass effect; when it does, these symptoms can be considered here unless rated by another organ system. The same holds true for residuals caused by surgery that was performed for a parathyroid disorder. In these cases, the adenoma or surgical residuals must give rise to problems that are sufficient to cause alterations in a person’s ADLs, allowing for inclusion in a class 1 or 2 parathyroid impairment. The only exception to this rule occurs when the symptoms are so significant that they are ratable by another organ system, for example, significant dysphagia that is assessed using the Digestive System chapter (Chapter 6).

10.5 Adrenal Cortex

The adrenal cortex synthesizes and secretes adreno-cortical hormones. These hormones participate in the regulation of electrolyte, water, carbohydrate, fat, and protein metabolism. They also affect the inflam-matory response, cell membrane permeability, and immunologic responses. In addition, these hormones play a role in the development and maintenance of secondary sexual characteristics. Impairment may result from either hypersecretion or hyposecretion of the cortical hormones.

10.5a Interpretation of Symptoms and Signs

Hypersecretion of adrenocortical hormones results from gland hyperplasia, tumors, or from pituitary ACTH hypersecretion (central Cushing’s disease). The symptoms and signs of adrenocortical disease may arise from hypersecretion of one or more of the following hormones: (1) glucocorticoids, (2) miner-alocorticoids, (3) androgens, and (4) estrogens. In some instances, there may be hypersecretion of hor-mones in one category and hyposecretion in another.

Among the diseases causing hypersecretion of the adrenocortical hormones are Cushing’s syndrome,

the adrenogenital syndrome, and primary aldoste-ronism. Hypersecretion of the adrenal cortex caused by hyperplasia may be associated with either a tumor of the anterior pituitary gland or one that arises outside the endocrine system and causes ectopic cor-ticotropin secretion. Iatrogenic Cushing’s syndrome caused by the use of supraphysiologic doses of glucocorticoids administered for systemic diseases, such as bronchial asthma, systemic lupus erythema-tosus, or rheumatoid arthritis, is the most common cause of adrenal hormonal excess. Excess aldoste-ronism (a mineralocorticoid) may be seen in up to 10% of hypertensive patients.

Hyposecretion of adrenocortical hormones may be primary, resulting from surgical removal of the adrenals or by destruction of the adrenals by autoimmune disease, infection (human immunode-ficiency virus [HIV], tuberculosis), or metastatic cancer. Alternatively, it may be secondary, result-ing from decreased production of corticotropin, or it may be tertiary, resulting from decreased production of corticotropin-releasing hormone by the hypothalamus. States of relative deficiency may be seen in individuals who have been or are receiving glucocorticoids; in other words, baseline levels may be normal, but stress levels of cortisol may be insufficient due to a variable degree of adrenal hyposecretion. Therapy is guided by the number of hormonal deficiencies, which may be single, as in hypoaldosteronism, or multiple, as in adrenocortical destruction. One normal adrenal gland can compensate for the loss of the other. Adrenal stimulation studies need to be performed in all individuals suspected of hyposecretory states to identify and pretreat these persons during times of stress.

10.5b Description of Clinical Studies

Clinical studies include (1) measurement of adreno-cortical hormones in the urine, such as free cortisol and aldosterone, and of hormones in the plasma, such as cortisol and aldosterone; (2) measurement of corticotropin, serum electrolytes, plasma glucose, and creatinine; (3) measurement of the effects of suppression and stimulation of adrenocortical func-tion; (4) roentgenography of the adrenal glands, CT, or MRI and (5) venous drainage sampling of both adrenal veins and inferior petrosal sinus vein for pituitary drainage. Techniques used to measure gonadal hormone levels (androgens and estrogens) are covered in Section 10.8.

10.5c Criteria for Rating Permanent Impairment due to Adrenal Cortex

Hypoadrenalism is usually a lifelong condition that requires long-term replacement therapy with glu-cocorticoids and/or mineralocorticoids for proven hormonal deficiencies. Individuals with mildly hypo-functional glands may prove difficult to identify. They may be fully functional on an everyday basis while taking medication but not be able to respond properly to the physical stress of fever, trauma, infection, or very warm weather. This impaired ability to respond to stress needs careful consideration. This consider-ation must also be given to those individuals receiving steroid therapy, as dysfunction of the adrenal glands may be seen in individuals who take as little as 5 mg of prednisone per day. Adrenal dysfunction can occur within a few days to a few weeks of continuous treat-ment and is caused by creation of a relative state of adrenal hyporesponsiveness due to suppression of the HPA axis. While not a primary manifestation of adre-nal disease, from a physiological standpoint, it mimics primary adrenal gland failure. Normal responsive-ness (recovery) is usually seen in these individuals, although it does not always occur. Recovery may be incomplete and may take as long as 1 year before an individual’s permanent status can be reliably assessed.

Gonadal hormone insufficiencies caused by an adrenal cortical disorder are not to be rated using

Section 10.8 (Gonads). Thus, any medications used to treat these abnormalities are included in the BOTC point total in this section. The only issue that can be rated separately is infertility, if this should occur because of the adrenal cortical disorder. This impairment should be assessed using Section 10.8, with apportionment, to avoid duplication in the impairment rating.

Note: Residual symptoms are those that are not rated by other organ systems. For example, a person with mildly excessive thirst or mild fatigue, when at MMI, should be rated using Table 10-8, whereas the cardiology chapter would be used to rate a person with residual hypertension. The biochemi-cal abnormalities are due to the adrenal hormones but not measurements of the actual hormone levels themselves.

Medications: Prednisone, 15 to 20 mg orally once a day; albuterol, 2 puffs 4 times a day; ipratropium, 2 puffs 4 times a day; cromolyn sodium, 2 puffs 4 times a day; beclomethasone, 4 puffs 4 times a day; theophylline, 150 mg 4 times a day; hydrochloro-thiazide, 12.5 mg per day; potassium, 10 mEq twice a day; calcium, 500 mg 3 times a day; and alendro-nate, 10 mg orally once a day.

BOTC: Two points are given for the most frequent medication, prednisone once daily. To this is added 2 dietary modification points for sodium restriction; there are no PBI points. The total number of points is 2 + 2 = 4 points.

Impairment Rating: Class 3, default level of 15%, based on history and her cushingoid habitus of more than a mild or moderate intensity. The BOTC is consistent with class 1 impairment, leading to adjust-ment of her rating downward to the bottom of the class to 10%. In this example, an indi-vidual is receiving a hormonal agent (prednisone) for an organ system other than her endocrinologic system. The effects of this hormonal agent, how-ever, are endocrinologic. The BOTC does not count the medications she takes for her asthma; these are accounted for separately according to the pulmonary rating system and subsequently combined.

10.6 Adrenal Medulla

10.6a Interpretation of Symptoms and Signs

The adrenal medulla synthesizes and secretes pri-marily epinephrine, which functions in the regula-tion of blood pressure and cardiac output and, to some extent, affects the intermediary metabolism of the body. The adrenal medulla is usually not essential to the maintenance of life or well-being.

Its absence may constitute a permanent impair-ment rating if an abnormality is detected in the individual’s ability to perform ADLs, especially in the response to stress. Hyperfunction of the adrenal medulla may be caused by pheochromocytomas or, rarely, by hyperplasia of the chromaffin cells. Pheochromocytomas may arise at any site in the body that has sympathetic nervous tissue. The pres-ence of a pheochromocytoma is usually associated with paroxysmal or sustained hypertension and may produce manifestations of coronary artery disease. Pheochromocytomas may be multiple in a patient and may occur in families in association with med-ullary carcinoma of the thyroid and hyperplasia of the parathyroids; this constitutes the syndrome of multiple endocrine neoplasia. Approximately 10% of pheochromocytomas are malignant.

10.6b Description of Clinical Studies

These techniques include (1) measurement of unme-tabolized urinary catecholamines, including total catecholamines, epinephrine, and norepinephrine, and of their degradation products in urine: vanillyl-mandelic acid, metanephrine, and normetanephrine; (2) measurement of the plasma free metanephrine and normetanephrine; (3) suppressive response of catecholamines to oral clonidine; (4) radiography of the adrenals by CT and MRI; and (5) nucleotide scanning.

10.6c Criteria for Evaluating Permanent Impairment due to the Adrenal Medulla

The usual cause of the impairment due to diseases of the adrenal medulla is the effect on various organ systems, not the endocrinologic signs or symptoms. When there are signs or symptoms that cannot be conveniently evaluated and rated by other organ sys-tems, a primary endocrinologic impairment may be assessed. The endocrinologic impairment is based on the interferences in an individual’s ADLs caused by those symptoms and the medications used to control those signs and/or symptoms. The impairment rating for this section is best done by estimation and extrap-olation, with the rationale explained in detail in the written report. Comparisons with other impairing processes, to compare the disturbances in ADLs, are helpful and are suggested. See Table 10-9.

10.7 Pancreas (Islets of Langerhans)

Insulin and glucagon are among the hormones secreted by the islets of Langerhans. Both hor-mones are required for the maintenance of normal metabolism of carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins. Permanent impairment may result from a deficiency or an excess of either hormone. Removal of normal pancreatic tissue during the resection of an islet cell neoplasm does not constitute an endocrine impair-ment if, after the operation, the individual’s carbohy-drate tolerance is normal.

10.7a Interpretation of Symptoms and Signs

Abnormalities of islet cell function may be manifest by high or low plasma glucose levels. Diabetes mel-litus is classified into 2 main groups: type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes. The complications of diabetes mellitus fall into 2 general categories: (1) those that are directly related to the degree of hyperglycemia

and (2) the chronic complications resulting from inadequate control of hyperglycemia and lipid metabolism over many years.

The diagnosis and characterization of diabetes has undergone significant changes over the past decade. Diabetes is currently diagnosed by a reproducible fasting blood glucose level equal to or greater than 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) or by abnormal glucose tolerance testing (2-hour postprandial glucose levels greater than 11.1 mmol/L [200 mg/dL]). Prediabetes is diagnosed by reproducible fasting blood glucose levels in the range of 5.6 to 6.9 mmol/L (100 to 125 mg/dL; impaired fasting glucose) or by 2-hour postprandial glucose levels in the range of 7.8 to 11.0 mmol/L (140 to 199 mg/dL; impaired glu-cose tolerance). Individuals with this condition are prone to the development of overt diabetes (5% to 10% per year) and are at significant risk of the car-diovascular complications of diabetes but not the ocular, neurologic, or renal complications. In 2003, there were approximately 17 million people in both groups in the United States, with approximately 33% of diabetic individuals being asymptomatic and undiagnosed. Almost all cases of prediabetes are undiagnosed.

A lack of insulin due to an autoimmune destruction of beta cell characterizes type 1 diabetes, whereas insulin resistance characterizes type 2 diabetes. Awareness has grown in the last 10 to 20 years of another condition associated with insulin resistance, the metabolic syndrome. This condition is associated with characteristic abnormalities of serum lipids, hypercoagulability, and central adiposity. Individuals with this condition are also at an enhanced risk of cardiovascular complications with its attendant mor-bidity and impairment.

If type 1 diabetes is untreated, severe hyperglycemia and ketonemia will develop, resulting in dehydra-tion, weight loss, and severe weakness, ultimately progressing into stupor, coma, and then death. This type of diabetes mellitus usually begins in young persons, but it may occur at any age. People with type 2 diabetes have traditionally been thought of as over 40 years old and overweight. However, there is a growing rise in traditional type 2 diabetes in younger populations. In the early years of this disease, these people do not have severe hyperglycemia and, indeed, may not experience any symptoms of the disease. In later years, when insulin production falls significantly, the hyperglycemic symptoms become more evident. However, the severe manifestations of hyperglycemia seen in type 1 diabetic patients are not usually seen in people with type 2 diabetes. The

principle chronic complications of diabetes mellitus that cause impairment are retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, and atherosclerosis.

Hypoglycemia occasionally causes impairment. It may result from excessive insulin that either is pro-duced endogenously or administered exogenously. Hypoglycemia may be manifest by weakness, sweat-ing, tachycardia, headache, confusion, muscular incoordination, blurred vision, loss of conscious-ness, and convulsions. Prolonged hypoglycemia or repeated severe attacks of hypoglycemia may lead to mental deterioration and brain damage.

10.7b Description of Clinical Studies

Clinical studies include but are not limited to: (1) determination of fasting and postprandial plasma glucose levels; (2) determination of glycated hemo-globin, or hemoglobin A1C (HbA1C), level; (3) mea-surements of levels of triglycerides, low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, and other lipids; (4) electrocardiogram or cardiac stress testing; (5) oph-thalmologic examination; (6) tests of renal function, including measurement of serum creatinine and urinary protein excretion; (7) Doppler testing of the peripheral circulation; (8) roentgenograms of the chest, gastrointestinal tract, pelvis, or extremities, including arteriograms; and (9) neurologic testing. Much of the impairment that results from diabetes is related to its long-term complications. Therefore, the examiner determines, in the patient with diabetes, the presence, or absence of vasculopathy, retinopa-thy, nephropathy, and neuropathy and rates those disorders appropriately. Impairments of other organ systems would be expressed as WPIs and then com-bined with an impairment percent resulting from the diabetes, by means of the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix.

10.7c Criteria for Evaluating Permanent Impairment due to Diabetes Mellitus

The endocrinologic impairment created by the dia-betic condition is best assessed by using the medica-tions given to control the condition as a surrogate of the severity of the disease. Impairment is based on the number of medications used to control this condition, the frequency that those medications are given, and the consequences of missing doses of the medication. Impairment also is based on the interfer-ences in a person’s daily activities by the disruptions created by the diabetes. These interferences include the need for dietary controls and the need to check blood glucose levels. Higher impairment values are given for the route of medication administra-tion since injections create more interference in a

person’s ADLs than does taking a pill orally. The same holds true for the maintenance and use of intra-body reservoirs for insulin. These elements are all addressed in the BOTC analysis.

The physical examination of the diabetic patient is normal except for the long-term consequences of this disease. These consequences are usually the effect of the vasculopathy found in diabetes, and they cor-relate with the control that the individual maintains over his or her disease over time. These vascular consequences can affect many different organ sys-tems and are assessed and rated by the appropriate chapter such as the chapter on cardiovascular dis-ease, renal disease, or ophthomlogic disease.

Thus, the physical examination is not used in the impairment assessment of the diabetic patient for rating the diabetes itself, although it serves as the basis for rating its complications through the various organ systems that the diabetes affects.

Objective testing is also a poor method of rating impairment in the diabetic patient for several rea-sons. Serum glucose measurements are inadequate to use as an impairment assessment tool. While valu-able in the day-to-day treatment of diabetes, they are more a reflection of the adequacy of the type and dose of medication or medications, compliance with dietary restrictions, and the effects of lifestyle, including the amount and regularity of exercise that the individual maintains as part of his or her daily routine. Serum insulin and glucagon measurements are of some value in the diagnosis of some glycemic conditions but are of no value for the impairment assessment.

Measurements of the HbA1c, while poor measures of the diabetic condition from an impairment rat-ing standpoint, can be used to detect the compli-ance with treatment regimens; significant elevations denote poor control. They can also be used to reflect the severity of the diabetes; the more severe the dis-ease, the more likely that a person will not be able to make all the adjustments necessary to maintain “tight” control. Inadequate control over the diabetes, as reflected in an elevated HbA1c, can be the result of improper medication use, poor dietary/exercise behavior, or inadequate medication prescription. Elevated levels are used as a discriminatory factor in the historical portion of the impairment assess-ment of diabetes to provide the impairment evaluator a method of assessing the degree of control that the individual is capable, or willing, of exerting over the disease process. The greater the elevation of the HbA1c, the lower the compliance and/or ability to

maintain a “tight control” over the diabetes. Poorer control of the diabetic condition is associated with greater cardiovascular, neurologic, and nephrologic complications and provides a marker of future impairment risk.

Thus, diabetes mellitus, from an endocrinologic standpoint, is assessed primarily by its interferences in a person’s ADLs through the need for medica-tion, the route of administration of the medication, the need for blood testing, and the need for dietary adjustments. Other factors in the historical assess-ment that are important to evaluate are the problems encountered due to hyperglycemia and hypoglyce-mia. Each condition can cause symptoms as well as hospitalizations. Not only an indication of the control that the individual maintains over his or her diabetes, hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia are used to assess the impairment created by the diabetes as a major indication of an interference in a person’s nor-mal lifestyle. Lastly, the HbA1c level is used to assess the degree of control, over time, of the diabetes. (See Table 10-10).

10.8 Gonads

In addition to producing gender-specific sex hor-mones that affect physical, sexual, development and behavior, the gonads produce either spermatozoa or ova. The major hormone of the testes is testosterone, whereas those of the ovaries are estrogen and pro-gesterone. In addition to the effects created by the normal aging process, dysfunction of the gonads can be caused by tumors, trauma, infection, chemother-apy, irradiation, autoimmune disease, abnormal XY chromatin, and surgical removal. Gonadal function may also vary with disorders of the HPA.

10.8a Interpretation of Symptoms and Signs

Precocious puberty in boys is accompanied by early and rapid somatic development and an increased rate of skeletal maturation and height velocity, but, paradoxically, it results in short adult height because of early closure of the epiphyses of the long bones. It may result from various central nervous system disorders, adrenal enzyme defects, virilizing tumors, or occasionally as a familial condition. Precocious puberty in girls may also be caused by various cen-tral nervous system disorders, as well as by ovarian and adrenal tumors. Often, a cause is not identified.

As in boys, precocious puberty in girls results in early and rapid somatic development and an increased rate of skeletal maturation and height velocity with, ultimately, a short adult stature. Some ovarian tumors may cause masculinization. Some adrenal enzyme defects and neoplasms, as well as some gonadal neoplasms, may produce contra-sexual precocity. Certain ovarian conditions produce irregular menstrual periods with heavy bleeding and anemia. Polycystic ovarian syndrome and several types of ovarian neoplasms may produce severe hirsutism and virilization, in addition to anovula-tion. Additionally, polycystic ovarian syndrome is associated with the metabolic syndrome; its systemic effects can be mitigated with oral hypoglycemic agents that increase the sensitivity to insulin.

Testicular hypofunction that occurs before adoles-cence results in eunuchoidism, which is accompa-nied by diminished sexual function, infertility, and failure to develop or maintain secondary sexual characteristics. Growth of the body extends beyond the usual age because of delayed epiphyseal clo-sure. Individuals with this condition usually lack endurance and strength. Testicular hypofunction that occurs in adulthood results in varying degrees of regression of secondary sexual characteristics, sexual function, strength, and endurance and may be accompanied by infertility.

Ovarian hypofunction, with onset before adoles-cence, may be characterized by primary amenor-rhea, anovulation, poor development of secondary sexual characteristics, and growth beyond the usual age because of delayed maturation of the skeleton.

Menopause is a natural occurrence in older women, but it also may follow surgical removal of the ova-ries. It may be accompanied by such symptoms as hot flashes, irritability, fatigue, headaches, mild cog-nitive difficulties, and sexual dysfunction.

10.8b Description of Clinical Studies

Clinical studies include but are not limited to: (1) measurements of plasma gonadotropins, prolac-tin, testosterone, estrogen, progesterone, DHEA-S, androstenedione, and occasionally 17-ketosteroids in the urine; (2) radiographic determinations of skeletal age in children and adolescents; (3) CT or MRI to evaluate the pituitary, adrenals, and ova-ries; (4) sex chromatin and chromosome studies; (5) testicular biopsy; (6) semen analysis; (7) vaginal cytologic examination; (8) colposcopy or laparos-copy; (9) endometrial biopsy; (10) ovarian biopsy; and (11) pelvic ultrasound in women.

10.8c Criteria for Rating Permanent Impairment due to Disorders of the Gonads

Care must be taken when assessing the reproduc-tive system of either the male or the female to avoid duplicating impairment, or more importantly, misusing this portion of the endocrine chapter and the sections of the renal chapter that deal with the sex organs (Sections 7.7 and 7.8). As can be seen from a perusal of these sections in the Urinary and Reproductive Systems chapter, Chapter 7 deals pri-marily with the anatomic aspects of these organs. This chapter deals primarily with the hormonal aspects of the reproductive system.

Infertility, however, has not been covered well in either Guides’ chapter in the past. It can be caused by an anatomic abnormality or a hormonal abnor-mality. Regardless of anatomic or hormonal cause, it can be a source of impairment for both men and women. When assessing impairment from an infertility standpoint, 2 primary issues need to be addressed: the age of the patient and the desire of that individual to reproduce. Men can be fertile seemingly forever; however, their desire to repro-duce may not be as lasting. This issue needs to be explained carefully in the impairment evaluation report before awarding any impairment based on infertility. Women, on the other hand, have a lim-ited expectancy for fertility, although with medical advancements in recent years, this issue has become more complex than in the past. With the proper use of exogenous hormones and stored ova, almost any woman, of any age, as long as she has an intact reproductive system, can be thought of as having the

potential of being fertile. These issues, in both men and women, are complex and beyond the scope and ability of this chapter.

Gonadal impairment is also present in those indi-viduals who have abnormalities of their body habitus (as discussed above) other than those causing repro-ductive abnormalities. These can be assessed using this portion of the Endocrinology chapter for these types of conditions that might not be otherwise rated or addressed. Impairment due to gonadal hormone insufficiencies are difficult to assess by using for-mulae similar to those found in other places in this chapter or other chapters in internal medicine. Thus, the method of placing an individual into a particular class is based on issues that are not otherwise rated by other organ systems and fall into the domain of hormonal deficiencies such as those caused by altered body habitus and infertility. Lack of treat-ment for gonadal impairment rarely results in imme-diate serious pathology, and many of the long-term effects can be treated directly, so treatment is virtu-ally never “required.” If the abnormality results in mild symptoms that do not affect ADLs or fertility, treatment is considered as “recommended”; if there are physical findings (such as masculinization or feminization of body habitus) treatment is classified as “highly recommended.”

Note:

1. Psychological issues, if present, are assessed in the Mental and Behavioral Disorders chapter (Chapter 14).

2. Class 3 impairment is based on factors such as the patient’s age and desire to remain reproduc-tive. If this leads to intermittent use of medica-tions or surgical procedures to achieve fertility, these are considered as part of the BOTC. This value should be combined with other endocrine impairments found either in this section or in other sections of this chapter. See Table 10-12.

10.9 Mammary Glands

The mammary glands are not endocrine organs but, for convenience sake, they are included in this chapter. The mammary glands make, store, and secrete milk. Absence of the mammary glands does not cause impairment of the whole person in males, but in premenopausal females it will prevent nursing. In some endocrine disorders, there may be galactorrhea in females and gynecomastia in males.

Gynecomastia in males may be accompanied by galactorrhea. The most significant impairment asso-ciated with disorders of the mammary glands, how-ever, is psychological due to cosmetic abnormalities and is rated by the Mental and Behavioral Disorders chapter (Chapter 14).

10.9a Criteria for Rating Permanent Impairment due to Mammary Gland Disorders

Impairment of the individual due to abnormalities of the mammary glands occurs in females of childbear-ing age with a reduced or absent ability to lactate, in an individual with galactorrhea sufficient to require the use of absorbent pads, and in a male with pain-ful gynecomastia that interferes with performance of ADLs. Mammary impairment is also seen in an individual who has sustained either a disfigurement or the removal of part or all of 1 or both breasts. This disfigurement can be acquired either on a traumatic or surgical basis. Cosmetic abnormalities of the breasts as a source of impairment must be associated with an alteration of the breast because of these mechanisms. Cosmetic abnormalities not attributable to trauma or the residuals of treatment are not ratable.

With the advent of the various forms of plastic surgi-cal procedures for the breasts, many of the surgical results seen in the past can be mitigated; any impair-ment rating should be postponed until the individual is at MMI, when the individual is stable and no fur-ther surgical intervention is planned. Impairment rat-ings for inadequate lactation are appropriate only for individuals who are capable and desirous of a future pregnancy. The BOTC is not a significant issue in mammary impairment.

Cosmetic abnormalities are rated at 1% to 5% WPI and can be assessed for both sexes. The actual number is based on the severity of the cosmetic abnormality, because anything more than a minor impairment meets the physical examination criteria for class 2 and results in the choice of the highest rating for class 1 (5%). Each breast is rated indepen-dently. As with all endocrinologic impairment, the impairment for each breast is combined before the final mammary impairment. Therefore, a maximum of 9% WPI can be assessed based on disfigurement.

10.10 Metabolic Bone Disease

Metabolic bone disease usually does not result in impairment unless there is fracture, pain, deformity, or peripheral nerve entrapment. Hyperparathyroidism, hypogonadism, glucocorticoid excess, hyperthyroidism, nutritional deficiencies, and certain drugs may cause osteoporosis that is reversible with treatment, and these are discussed

elsewhere, as are multiple myeloma and other malig-nancies. The treatment of renal osteodystrophy may be highly successful, but even after renal transplan-tation, bone disease may persist. To prevent progres-sive skeletal deterioration, it may be necessary to employ continuous treatment for primary osteopo-rosis, hypogonadism, Paget’s disease, and vitamin D-resistant osteomalacia. Permanent deformity may result from rickets, osteoporotic fractures, and osteo-genesis imperfecta.

10.10a Interpretation of Symptoms and Signs

Metabolic bone disease is usually asymptomatic unless complications occur, such as fractures or dis-orders of calcium metabolism leading to neurologic symptoms or renal disease.

10.10b Description of Clinical Studies

Clinical studies include but are not limited to: (1) dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA); (2) biochemical markers such as alkaline phospha-tase, osteocalcin, and collagen cross-links; (3) uri-nary calcium excretion; (4) radiographs and bone scans; and (5) bone biopsy.

10.10c Criteria for Rating Permanent Impairment due to Metabolic Bone Disease

Impairment of the whole person should be consid-ered based on the clinical history and the objective findings on diagnostic testing (T score). The BOTC

varies immensely based on patient preference and can be minimal.

Because of the wide variations in dosing (from once a day to once a year), the BOTC points are intrinsically incorporated into the scheme found in Table 10-14. It is consequently included in the rating. Impairment from fracture, spinal collapse, or other complications of metabolic bone disease is discussed in the chapters on the musculoskeletal system (Chapters 15 to 17) and in Pain-Related Impairment (Chapter 3). In general, the impairment percents shown in the Guides make allow-ance for the pain that may accompany the impairing conditions, and, as such, no separate rating is incorpo-rated into Table 10-14.

Any associated loss of motion or function caused by the osteoporosis, is rated by the appropriate sections in the chapters on the musculoskeletal system.

Current Symptoms: Persistent fatigue, mild nausea, polyuria, and nocturia.

Physical Exam: Normal.
